ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Anopheles mosquitoes are the sole vectors of human malaria. Only female Anopheles transmit Plasmodium sporozoites during a blood meal, linking vector biology to disease risk.

sections.p: Anopheles are a genus of night‑biting mosquitoes found in tropical and subtropical regions. Their biology determines where malaria can occur and guides control strategies.
b: Females require a blood meal to develop eggs.
Only Anopheles (not Culex or Aedes) transmit human malaria.

sections.p: Adult Anopheles have a characteristic resting posture with the abdomen at an angle to the surface and palps longer than those of other genera.
b: Larvae develop in clean, sunlit water.

sections.p: Female Anopheles ingest Plasmodium gametocytes during a blood meal, which develop into sporozoites in the mosquito’s salivary glands. A subsequent bite injects sporozoites into the human host.
b: Mosquito = definitive host; human = intermediate host.
Sporozoites travel to liver → hepatic schizogony.

t.b: How many infectious bites per person per time; high EIR predicts outbreak risk.
Identifies breeding sites; guides vector control when labs unavailable.

sections.p: Anopheles transmits Plasmodium falciparum, vivax, ovale, malariae, and knowlesi, causing malaria with a spectrum from uncomplicated fever to severe organ dysfunction.
b: Uncomplicated malaria: fever, chills, headache, anemia.
Severe malaria: cerebral involvement, severe anemia, renal failure, hypoglycemia.

sections.p: Diagnosis focuses on detecting Plasmodium in the patient, not the mosquito, but understanding vector exposure informs pre‑test probability.
b: Thick and thin blood smears remain gold standard.
Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detect HRP2 or pLDH antigens.

t.b: Confirms species and parasite density; high density (>100,000/µL) indicates severe disease.
Quick rule‑in for P. falciparum; may be false‑negative with HRP2 gene deletions.
Detects low‑level infection and mixed species; used when microscopy/RDT inconclusive.

sections.p: Management combines antimalarial therapy with vector control. Treat the parasite first, then prevent further bites.
b: Artemisinin‑based combination therapy (ACT) for uncomplicated falciparum malaria – kills blood‑stage parasites.
Intravenous artesunate for severe malaria – rapid parasite clearance, avoids quinine toxicity.
Insecticide‑treated nets (ITNs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS) reduce exposure.

sections.p: Key points that often appear in exams.
b: Only female Anopheles transmit malaria – remember the “only female” rule.
Severe malaria criteria: cerebral signs, >5% parasitemia, renal failure, severe anemia, hypoglycemia.
HRP2‑RDT false‑negative in areas with HRP2‑deleted P. falciparum.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anemia (Hb <5 g/dL) or respiratory distress
Renal failure, persistent vomiting, or hypoglycemia

faq.q: Why are only female Anopheles vectors?
faq.a: Only females need blood for egg development, so they bite and can inoculate sporozoites.
No, Culex and Aedes do not support Plasmodium development; they are vectors for other diseases.

faq.q: What if a rapid test is negative but suspicion remains high?
faq.a: Perform microscopy or PCR; consider HRP2 gene deletion and repeat testing.

exam: Explain the life cycle of Plasmodium in the Anopheles mosquito and why only females transmit the parasite.
List the WHO criteria for severe malaria and describe the immediate management steps.
Describe two vector‑control measures and the rationale behind each.
